claim: T cells play a critical role in the adaptive immune response, recognizing peptide antigens presented on the cell surface by major histocompatibility complex (MHC) proteins.
source: T cells play a critical role in the adaptive immune response, recognizing peptide antigens presented on the cell surface by major histocompatibility complex (MHC) proteins.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about T cell function in adaptive immunity.

claim: Traditional assays for testing peptides of interest for MHC binding are limited in throughput.
source: traditional assays for testing peptides of interest for MHC binding are limited in throughput.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and established understanding in the field.

claim: The yeast display-based platform can assess the binding of tens of thousands of user-defined peptides in a high-throughput manner.
source: Here, we present a yeast display-based platform for assessing the binding of tens of thousands of user-defined peptides in a high-throughput manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the experimental data showing library sizes of 11,040 and 12,672 peptides tested.

claim: The approach was applied to assess a tiled library covering the SARS-CoV-2 proteome for binding to human class II MHCs, including HLA-DR401, -DR402, and -DR404.
source: We apply this approach to assess a tiled library covering the SARS-CoV-2 proteome and four dengue virus serotypes for binding to human class II MHCs, including HLA-DR401, -DR402, and -DR404.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the results section with experimental data.

claim: The approach was applied to assess four dengue virus serotypes for binding to human class II MHCs, including HLA-DR401, -DR402, and -DR404.
source: We apply this approach to assess a tiled library covering the SARS-CoV-2 proteome and four dengue virus serotypes for binding to human class II MHCs, including HLA-DR401, -DR402, and -DR404.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and demonstrated in the results section with dengue library data.

claim: The peptide datasets show broad agreement with previously described MHC-binding motifs.
source: While the peptide datasets show broad agreement with previously described MHC-binding motifs, they additionally reveal experimentally validated computational false positives and false negatives.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of sequence logos with previously reported motifs and citations to prior work.

claim: The peptide datasets reveal experimentally validated computational false positives and false negatives.
source: While the peptide datasets show broad agreement with previously described MHC-binding motifs, they additionally reveal experimentally validated computational false positives and false negatives.
evidence: This is demonstrated through fluorescence polarization experiments comparing yeast display results with NetMHCIIpan4.0 predictions.

claim: Class II MHC molecules are expressed primarily on professional antigen-presenting cells.
source: Class II MHC molecules (MHC-II) are expressed primarily on professional antigen-presenting cells, and are recognized by antigen-specific CD4+ T cells that drive the coordination of innate and adaptive immune responses (Chaplin, 2010; Swain et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Class II MHC molecules are recognized by antigen-specific CD4+ T cells that drive the coordination of innate and adaptive immune responses.
source: Class II MHC molecules (MHC-II) are expressed primarily on professional antigen-presenting cells, and are recognized by antigen-specific CD4+ T cells that drive the coordination of innate and adaptive immune responses (Chaplin, 2010; Swain et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MHC-II molecules have an open peptide-binding groove, allowing for display of long peptides, consisting of a nine amino acid 'core' flanked by a variable number of additional residues on each side.
source: MHC-II molecules have an open peptide-binding groove, allowing for display of long peptides, consisting of a nine amino acid 'core' flanked by a variable number of additional residues on each side (Jones et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about MHC-II molecules supported by citation.

claim: Therapeutics to generate antigen-specific T cell responses have shown great promise in cancer.
source: In fact, therapeutics to generate antigen-specific T cell responses have shown great promise in cancer (Keskin et al., 2019; Ott et al., 2017) and infectious disease (Gambino et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Therapeutics to generate antigen-specific T cell responses have shown great promise in infectious disease.
source: In fact, therapeutics to generate antigen-specific T cell responses have shown great promise in cancer (Keskin et al., 2019; Ott et al., 2017) and infectious disease (Gambino et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Initial experimental methods for determining peptide binding to MHC relied upon the analysis of synthesized candidate peptides via MHC stability or functional assays.
source: Initial experimental methods for determining peptide binding to MHC relied upon the analysis of synthesized candidate peptides via MHC stability or functional assays, and can produce high-confidence data, but can be difficult to scale beyond a small number of candidate peptides (Altmann and Boyton, 2020; Justesen et al., 2009; Mateus et al., 2020; Sidney et al., 2010; Yin and Stern, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous methodological work.

claim: Initial experimental methods for determining peptide binding to MHC can produce high-confidence data, but can be difficult to scale beyond a small number of candidate peptides.
source: Initial experimental methods for determining peptide binding to MHC relied upon the analysis of synthesized candidate peptides via MHC stability or functional assays, and can produce high-confidence data, but can be difficult to scale beyond a small number of candidate peptides (Altmann and Boyton, 2020; Justesen et al., 2009; Mateus et al., 2020; Sidney et al., 2010; Yin and Stern, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous methodological work.

claim: Mass spectrometry-based approaches are not necessarily quantitative measures of presented peptide affinity or abundance.
source: However, mass spectrometry-based approaches are not necessarily quantitative measures of presented peptide affinity or abundance, although there have been advances in quantitation using internal standards (Stopfer et al., 2021; Stopfer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations discussing limitations and advances in mass spectrometry quantitation.

claim: There have been advances in quantitation of mass spectrometry-based approaches using internal standards.
source: However, mass spectrometry-based approaches are not necessarily quantitative measures of presented peptide affinity or abundance, although there have been advances in quantitation using internal standards (Stopfer et al., 2021; Stopfer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent methodological advances.

claim: The peptides endogenously expressed by a cell can crowd out exogenously examined peptides of interest in mass spectrometry approaches.
source: Additionally, the peptides endogenously expressed by a cell can crowd out exogenously examined peptides of interest, and mass spectrometry approaches typically require large numbers of input cells (Abelin et al., 2019; Abelin et al., 2017; Parker et al., 2021; Purcell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations discussing limitations of mass spectrometry approaches.

claim: Mass spectrometry approaches typically require large numbers of input cells.
source: Additionally, the peptides endogenously expressed by a cell can crowd out exogenously examined peptides of interest, and mass spectrometry approaches typically require large numbers of input cells (Abelin et al., 2019; Abelin et al., 2017; Parker et al., 2021; Purcell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations discussing limitations of mass spectrometry approaches.

claim: Computational approaches for peptide-MHC binding prediction have advanced markedly over the past decade.
source: In addition to experimental advances, computational approaches for peptide-MHC binding prediction have advanced markedly over the past decade. These developments are due to algorithmic advances (O'Donnell et al., 2020; Racle et al., 2019; Reynisson et al., 2020; Zeng and Gifford, 2019) and the availability of large, high-quality training data (Abelin et al., 2019; Abelin et al., 2017; Rappazzo et al., 2020; Reynisson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent algorithmic and data advances.

claim: The predictive power for individual peptides often remains imperfect relative to experimental measurements despite improvements in predicting peptide binding to MHC.
source: However, despite the improvements in predicting peptide binding to MHC in a broad sense, the predictive power for individual peptides often remains imperfect relative to experimental measurements (Rappazzo et al., 2020; Zhao and Sher, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations discussing limitations of prediction algorithms.

claim: Each protein was windowed into peptides of 15 amino acids in length, with a step size of 1 to cover every possible 15mer peptide in the protein.
source: Each protein was windowed into peptides of 15 amino acids in length, with a step size of 1 to cover every possible 15mer peptide in the protein (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: The final library contained 11,040 unique peptides.
source: The final library contained 11,040 unique peptides, with 99% of the designed peptides present in each cloned yeast library, as assessed by next-generation sequencing.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of library construction and sequencing.

claim: 99% of the designed peptides were present in each cloned yeast library, as assessed by next-generation sequencing.
source: The final library contained 11,040 unique peptides, with 99% of the designed peptides present in each cloned yeast library, as assessed by next-generation sequencing.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of library construction and sequencing.

claim: Three rounds of selection were iteratively performed on the undoped library.
source: Three rounds of selection were iteratively performed.
evidence: This is directly stated in the methods description.

claim: The pre-selection Myc-positive population for the undoped HLA-DR401 library started at 29.3% and converged to 65.0% in Round 2 and 74.1% in Round 3.
source: Representative enrichment of yeast expressing Myc-tagged peptides can be seen in Figure 1c ('undoped library'), for the library displayed by HLA-DR401. Here, the pre-selection Myc-positive population starts at 29.3% and quickly converges, with 65.0% positive in the pre-selection Round 2 population and 74.1% in the pre-selection Round 3 population.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1c flow cytometry data.

claim: The defined library was doped into a 500-fold excess of null library.
source: We doped our defined peptide library into a 500-fold excess of null library, such that each peptide member was represented at approximately the same frequency (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: Four rounds of selection were performed on the doped library.
source: We performed four rounds of selection on the doped library.
evidence: This is directly stated in the methods description.

claim: The initial pre-selection stain for the doped library was 1.6%.
source: Because of the excess of null yeast, the initial pre-selection stain is low (1.6%) compared to the initial undoped library (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Of the 11,040 peptides in the library, 2467 enriched in both the doped and undoped libraries displayed by HLA-DR401.
source: Of the 11,040 peptides in the library, 2467 enriched in both the doped and undoped libraries displayed by HLA-DR401 (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: An additional 1252 peptides enriched in the doped library only for HLA-DR401.
source: An additional 1252 enriched in the doped library only and 797 enriched in the undoped library only.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of the selection analysis.

claim: 797 peptides enriched in the undoped library only for HLA-DR401.
source: An additional 1252 enriched in the doped library only and 797 enriched in the undoped library only.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of the selection analysis.

claim: The strongest determinant of peptide affinity for an MHC is the nine amino acid stretch sitting within the peptide-binding groove.
source: Classically, the strongest determinant of peptide affinity for an MHC is the nine amino acid stretch sitting within the peptide-binding groove (Jones et al., 2006; Stern et al., 1994), although proximal peptide flanking residues can also affect binding (Lovitch et al., 2006; O'Brien et al., 2008; Zavala-Ruiz et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Proximal peptide flanking residues can affect MHC binding.
source: Classically, the strongest determinant of peptide affinity for an MHC is the nine amino acid stretch sitting within the peptide-binding groove (Jones et al., 2006; Stern et al., 1994), although proximal peptide flanking residues can also affect binding (Lovitch et al., 2006; O'Brien et al., 2008; Zavala-Ruiz et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A given 9mer is present in seven overlapping 15mer peptides in the libraries.
source: In our libraries, a given 9mer is present in seven overlapping 15mer peptides, and we calculate how many of these seven 15mers have enriched.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the library design with 15mer peptides and step size of 1.

claim: A cutoff for high-confidence 9mer enrichment was defined as five out of seven 9mer-containing sequences enriching.
source: Thus, we define a cutoff for high-confidence 9mer enrichment of five out of seven 9mer-containing sequences enriching.
evidence: This is directly stated as a methodological decision.

claim: Of the 2467 peptides which enriched in both the doped and undoped libraries for HLA-DR401, 1791 also contain a 9mer sequence which enriched in five or more peptides of the seven neighboring sequences containing it.
source: Of the 2467 peptides which enriched in both the doped and undoped libraries for HLA-DR401, 1791 also contain a 9mer sequence which enriched in five or more peptides of the seven neighboring sequences containing it (Figure 2a)
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The peptide motif for HLA-DR401 enriched peptides is consistent with previously reported motifs: hydrophobic amino acids are preferred at P1, acidic residues at P4, polar residues at P6, and small residues at P9.
source: The peptide motif is consistent with previously reported motifs for HLA-DR401 (Abelin et al., 2019; Rappazzo et al., 2020): hydrophobic amino acids are preferred at P1, acidic residues at P4, polar residues at P6, and small residues at P9.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by comparison with cited previous work and shown in Figure 2c.

claim: HLA-DR401 differs from HLA-DR402 at four amino acids.
source: HLA-DR401 differs from HLA-DR402 at four amino acids and from HLA-DR404 at two amino acids, with all polymorphisms located in the beta chain.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: HLA-DR401 differs from HLA-DR404 at two amino acids.
source: HLA-DR401 differs from HLA-DR402 at four amino acids and from HLA-DR404 at two amino acids, with all polymorphisms located in the beta chain.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: All polymorphisms between HLA-DR401, HLA-DR402, and HLA-DR404 are located in the beta chain.
source: HLA-DR401 differs from HLA-DR402 at four amino acids and from HLA-DR404 at two amino acids, with all polymorphisms located in the beta chain.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: HLA-DR402 and HLA-DR404 share an amino acid distinct from HLA-DR401 affecting the P1 pocket (Gly86Val), resulting in a preference for smaller hydrophobic residues.
source: HLA-DR402 and HLA-DR404 share an amino acid distinct from HLA-DR401 affecting the P1 pocket (Gly86Val), resulting in a preference for smaller hydrophobic residues (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3a, with inference about binding preference based on structural knowledge.

claim: Three polymorphisms in HLA-DR402 affect P4, P5, and P7 compared to HLA-DR401 (Leu67Ile, Gln70Asp, and Lys71Glu).
source: Three polymorphisms in HLA-DR402 affect P4, P5, and P7 compared to HLA-DR401 (Leu67Ile, Gln70Asp, and Lys71Glu), while HLA-DR404 has only one (Lys71Arg).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: HLA-DR404 has one polymorphism affecting P7 compared to HLA-DR401 (Lys71Arg).
source: Three polymorphisms in HLA-DR402 affect P4, P5, and P7 compared to HLA-DR401 (Leu67Ile, Gln70Asp, and Lys71Glu), while HLA-DR404 has only one (Lys71Arg).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Three of the most preferred P4 residues for binding HLA-DR402 (Trp, His, and Met) are all low abundance in the SARS-CoV-2 proteome (Trp 1.1%, His 1.9%, Met 2.2%).
source: Indeed, three of the most preferred P4 residues for binding HLA-DR402, Trp, His, and Met (Rappazzo et al., 2020), are all low abundance in the SARS-CoV-2 proteome (Trp 1.1%, His 1.9%, Met 2.2%).
evidence: This is directly stated with calculated amino acid frequencies from the SARS-CoV-2 proteome.

claim: A randomized peptide library for HLA-DR402 had a higher representation of Trp, His, and Met (Trp 3.8%, His 2.9%, Met 3.8%) compared to the SARS-CoV-2 proteome.
source: In comparison, a randomized peptide library for HLA-DR402 (Rappazzo et al., 2020) had a higher representation of these amino acids (Trp 3.8%, His 2.9%, Met 3.8%).
evidence: This is directly stated with calculated amino acid frequencies from a previous study.

claim: Of the 2467 enriched peptides from the HLA-DR401 library, 1610 peptides bound native 9mer cores without using any linker sequence residues in the 9mer core.
source: Based on our register inference, of the 2467 enriched peptides from the HLA-DR401 library, 1610 peptides bound native 9mer cores without using any linker sequence residues in the 9mer core, which is consistent with theoretical ratios of possible native and non-native cores for a given 9mer (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of register inference analysis.

claim: Of the 1610 HLA-DR401 peptides which enriched using a native 9mer core, there are 563 unique 9mer cores identified through register inference.
source: Of the 1610 HLA-DR401 peptides which enriched using a native 9mer core, there are 563 unique 9mer cores identified through register inference.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of register inference analysis.

claim: All eight 'Yeast-Enriched Binders', which enriched in the yeast display assay but were not predicted to bind via NetMHCIIpan4.0, showed some degree of binding, with IC50 values distributed from 14 nM to 18 µM.
source: All eight 'Yeast-Enriched Binders', which enriched in the yeast display assay but were not predicted to bind via NetMHCIIpan4.0, showed some degree of binding, with IC50 values distributed from 14 nM (higher affinity than the HA control peptide) to 18 µM (weak, but measurable, binding).
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Table 2.

claim: NetMHCIIpan4.0 predictions on the peptides identified via yeast display proved highly sensitive to the length or content of the flanking sequences.
source: Interestingly, NetMHCIIpan4.0 predictions on the peptides identified via yeast display proved highly sensitive to the length or content of the flanking sequences: if we repeat predictions on only the antigen-derived 15mer sequences without the flanking sequences, NetMHCIIpan4.0 recovers four of its former false-negative peptides (Table 3; peptides listed at the top in each section of the table).
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison of predictions with and without flanking sequences shown in Table 3.

claim: Of the eight 'Yeast-Enriched Binders' in Table 2, six contain cysteine residues.
source: Of the eight 'Yeast-Enriched Binders' in Table 2, six contain cysteine residues, which have been shown to be systematically absent from other datasets, including those from monoallelic mass spectrometry (Abelin et al., 2019; Barra et al., 2018), yet present in yeast display-derived datasets (Rappazzo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated and can be verified from Table 2 sequences.

claim: Cysteine-containing peptides have been shown to be systematically absent from monoallelic mass spectrometry datasets.
source: Of the eight 'Yeast-Enriched Binders' in Table 2, six contain cysteine residues, which have been shown to be systematically absent from other datasets, including those from monoallelic mass spectrometry (Abelin et al., 2019; Barra et al., 2018), yet present in yeast display-derived datasets (Rappazzo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cysteine-containing peptides are present in yeast display-derived datasets.
source: Of the eight 'Yeast-Enriched Binders' in Table 2, six contain cysteine residues, which have been shown to be systematically absent from other datasets, including those from monoallelic mass spectrometry (Abelin et al., 2019; Barra et al., 2018), yet present in yeast display-derived datasets (Rappazzo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation and demonstrated in the current study's data.

claim: Two cysteine-containing 'Agreed Non-Binders' showed no affinity for HLA-DR401, suggesting that cysteine itself is not causing non-specific binding.
source: To test for non-specific binding due to cysteine, two cysteine-containing 'Agreed Non-Binders' were also tested and showed no affinity for HLA-DR401, suggesting that cysteine itself is not causing non-specific binding.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Table 2.

claim: The highest affinity binder (14 nM) in the fluorescence polarization dataset contained cysteine and was missed by NetMHCIIpan4.0 predictions.
source: In the fluorescence polarization dataset, the highest affinity binder (14 nM) contained cysteine and was missed by NetMHCIIpan4.0 predictions (Eluted Ligand mode %Rank: 71 [with flanking residues] and 28 [without flanking residues]).
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of fluorescence polarization experiments and NetMHCIIpan4.0 predictions shown in Table 2.

claim: Libraries containing 12,672 dengue-derived peptides were generated, covering the entire proteomes of dengue serotypes 1–4.
source: To profile and compare MHC binding across serotypes, we generated libraries containing 12,672 dengue-derived peptides, covering the entire proteomes of dengue serotypes 1–4.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of library construction.

claim: The dengue libraries on HLA-DR401 and HLA-DR402 had coverage of 98% and 96% of the dengue library members after construction, respectively.
source: These libraries were on HLA-DR401 and HLA-DR402 and had coverage of 98% and 96% of the dengue library members after construction, respectively (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of library construction and sequencing.

claim: Antibody-dependent enhancement in dengue viruses results in more severe disease upon second infection with a different dengue virus serotype.
source: We additionally apply this approach to screen proteomes from serotypes 1–4 of dengue viruses, in which antibody-dependent enhancement results in more severe disease upon second infection with a different dengue virus serotype (Guzman et al., 2016), and thus represents a potential important application area for T cell-directed therapeutics.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dengue virus pathology supported by citation.

claim: Peptides which both enriched in yeast display and were predicted by NetMHCIIpan4.0 to bind ('Agreed Binders') all showed IC50 values consistent with binding, each with IC50 < 2.2 µM.
source: Peptides which both enriched in yeast display and were predicted by NetMHCIIpan4.0 to bind ('Agreed Binders') all showed IC50 values consistent with binding, each with IC50 < 2.2 µM.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Table 2.

claim: Peptides which were agreed non-binders showed no affinity for HLA-DR401, with IC50 > 50 µM.
source: Similarly, peptides which were agreed non-binders showed no affinity for HLA-DR401, with IC50 > 50 µM.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Table 2.

claim: All five offset peptides exhibit some binding, with IC50 values below 13 µM.
source: All five offset peptides exhibit some binding, with IC50 values below 13 µM.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Table 3.

claim: Each offset peptide is lower affinity than its overlapping centered counterpart.
source: Each peptide is lower affinity than its overlapping centered counterpart, illustrating effects of flanking residues on peptide binding, although some over-estimation of these effects in NetMHCIIpan4.0 predictions are present.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Table 3.

claim: Of three 'NetMHC-Predicted Binders', one bound to HLA-DR401 (IC50 475 nM), while two showed minimal binding with IC50 > 35 µM.
source: Of these, one bound to HLA-DR401 (IC50 475 nM), while two showed minimal binding with IC50 > 35 µM, which is above the maximum 20 µM concentration tested.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Table 2.

claim: Yeast display libraries can generate data for diverse objectives.
source: Defined yeast display libraries can generate data for diverse objectives.
evidence: This is demonstrated through application to both SARS-CoV-2 and dengue virus proteomes.

claim: Dengue viruses typically cause most severe disease after a second infection with a serotype different from the first infection, due to antibody-dependent enhancement.
source: Dengue viruses typically cause most severe disease after a second infection with a serotype different from the first infection, due to antibody-dependent enhancement (Guzman et al., 2016), which makes T cell-directed therapeutics a potentially attractive means of combating disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dengue virus pathology supported by citation.

claim: T cell-directed therapeutics are a potentially attractive means of combating dengue disease.
source: Dengue viruses typically cause most severe disease after a second infection with a serotype different from the first infection, due to antibody-dependent enhancement (Guzman et al., 2016), which makes T cell-directed therapeutics a potentially attractive means of combating disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the antibody-dependent enhancement problem in dengue.

claim: The yeast display approach benefits from recent advances in next-generation sequencing and pooled oligonucleotide synthesis.
source: When compared to previously described yeast display approaches to identify peptides binding to MHC-II molecules, our approach benefits from recent advances in next-generation sequencing and pooled oligonucleotide synthesis.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with previous methods.

claim: Other library generation methods for peptide-MHC-II binding have relied on synthetic peptides, randomized DNA-encoded peptides, or digested DNA from amplified viral genomes, which are impractical for comprehensive assessment of defined proteome-scale libraries.
source: Other library generation methods for peptide-MHC-II binding have relied on synthetic peptides (Liu et al., 2021a), randomized, DNA-encoded peptides (Rappazzo et al., 2020), or digested DNA from amplified viral genomes (Wen et al., 2008), which are impractical for comprehensive assessment of defined proteome-scale libraries.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with previous methods supported by citations.

claim: Weak binding peptides have been reported to be less immunodominant than strong MHC-binding peptides.
source: Weak binding peptides have been reported to be less immunodominant than strong MHC-binding peptides (Burger et al., 2021; Lazarski et al., 2005; Wu et al., 2019); however, there are also examples of weak MHC-binding peptides which can elicit T cell responses and be of clinical relevance in disease contexts, including in autoimmunity and cancer (Latek et al., 2000; Levisetti et al., 2008; Valmori et al., 1998; Zarour et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There are examples of weak MHC-binding peptides which can elicit T cell responses and be of clinical relevance in disease contexts, including in autoimmunity and cancer.
source: Weak binding peptides have been reported to be less immunodominant than strong MHC-binding peptides (Burger et al., 2021; Lazarski et al., 2005; Wu et al., 2019); however, there are also examples of weak MHC-binding peptides which can elicit T cell responses and be of clinical relevance in disease contexts, including in autoimmunity and cancer (Latek et al., 2000; Levisetti et al., 2008; Valmori et al., 1998; Zarour et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The overlapping peptides in the library were useful for identifying enriched cores, especially when combined with register inference to identify consensus cores shared between these overlapping peptides.
source: The overlapping peptides in our library were useful for identifying enriched cores, especially when combined with our register inference to identify consensus cores shared between these overlapping peptides.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis approach.

claim: NetMHCIIpan4.0 exhibits a sensitivity to length and register, which may cause users to miss binders, albeit potentially of lower affinity.
source: NetMHCIIpan4.0 exhibits a sensitivity to length and register, which may cause users to miss binders, albeit potentially of lower affinity.
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison of predictions with experimental data in Tables 2 and 3.

claim: NetMHCIIpan4.0 correctly ranked the affinities of the overlapping peptides tested.
source: Of the overlapping peptides we tested to study this phenomenon, NetMHCIIpan4.0 correctly ranked the affinities of the overlapping peptides (Table 3), but missed binders.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of comparing predictions with fluorescence polarization data in Table 3.

claim: Comparison with yeast display datasets highlights several non-binding peptides predicted by NetMHCIIpan4.0 to be binders.
source: Comparison with yeast display datasets also highlights several non-binding peptides predicted by NetMHCIIpan4.0 to be binders.
evidence: This is demonstrated through fluorescence polarization experiments showing false positive predictions in Table 2.

claim: Coupling yeast display approach with computational predictions can be useful for identifying false positive predicted peptides in order to correctly prioritize peptides of interest.
source: Coupling this yeast display approach with computational predictions can be useful for identifying false positive predicted peptides in order to correctly prioritize peptides of interest.
evidence: This is inferred from the complementary nature of the two approaches demonstrated in the results.

claim: Design of defined libraries with sources of redundancy, such as overlapping peptides, was critical for determining binders with higher degrees of confidence.
source: Design of defined libraries with sources of redundancy, such as overlapping peptides, was critical for determining binders with higher degrees of confidence and allowed us to apply stringent cutoffs for individual peptides.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis approach.

claim: Overlapping peptides allowed accounting for construct-specific confounding effects, such as the peptides binding using non-native residues in the linker.
source: Overlapping peptides allowed us to account for construct-specific confounding effects, such as the peptides binding using non-native residues in the linker.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis approach.

claim: Comparison of unbiased and proteome-derived libraries highlights how aggregate motifs may be affected by underlying amino acid preferences found in protein sequences themselves.
source: Additionally, our comparison of unbiased and proteome-derived libraries highlights how aggregate motifs may be affected by underlying amino acid preferences found in protein sequences themselves, which may inadvertently disfavor sequences that can bind strongly to MHC molecules yet consist of amino acid covariates that are not as commonly found in proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of amino acid frequencies in different library types.

claim: The yeast display approach can be used to study MHC binding between similar viruses, highlighting regions where mutations disrupt binding as well as regions where binding is unperturbed.
source: Further, this approach can be used to study MHC binding between similar viruses, as done with the dengue proteomes and the spike proteins from SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV, highlighting regions where mutations disrupt binding as well as regions where binding is unperturbed.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the comparative analysis shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: The method can be rapidly adapted to study future sequences if pathogens evolve over time.
source: This method can also be rapidly adapted to study future sequences if pathogens evolve over time.
evidence: This is inferred from the flexible nature of the library design approach.

claim: NetMHCIIpan4.0 prediction and yeast display selections identified sets of non-overlapping misses.
source: NetMHCIIpan4.0 prediction and yeast display selections identified sets of non-overlapping misses, highlighting a utility for both.
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison of predictions with experimental data in Tables 2 and Figure 4.

claim: All agreed binders and non-binders matched fluorescence polarization results.
source: Additionally, all agreed binders and non-binders matched fluorescence polarization results, suggesting a consensus of yeast display enrichment and algorithmic prediction provide high-confidence results.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Table 2.

claim: A consensus of yeast display enrichment and algorithmic prediction provide high-confidence results.
source: Additionally, all agreed binders and non-binders matched fluorescence polarization results, suggesting a consensus of yeast display enrichment and algorithmic prediction provide high-confidence results.
evidence: This is inferred from the perfect agreement between agreed binders/non-binders and fluorescence polarization results.

claim: The yeast display platform to assess peptide-MHC binding can be used to design high-throughput assays to test peptide immunogenicity in clinical samples.
source: In another application, our platform to assess peptide-MHC binding can be used to design high-throughput assays to test peptide immunogenicity in clinical samples (Klinger et al., 2015; Snyder et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative application supported by citations to related work.

claim: Defined yeast display peptide libraries can be readily applied to identification of T cell ligands and present an opportunity for identifying unknown ligands from orphan TCRs known to respond to a proteome of interest.
